question: Alma deals combat damage to Nico with their [Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer]. They exile [Deceit] from Nico's library. Can Alma evoke Deceit?
answer:
Yes. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's ability says "Until end of turn, you may cast that card," which is an effect permitting Alma to cast Deceit from exile. Evoke is "a static ability that functions in any zone from which the card with evoke can be cast" (702.74a), so once Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer makes Deceit castable from exile, Deceit's evoke ability applies there too and Alma may pay {U/B}{U/B} (two mana, each either blue or black) instead of Deceit's mana cost of {4}{U/B}{U/B}. question: Amiyah taps their [The One Ring], which currently has no burden counters on it, to draw a card. Before that resolves Nico casts [Soul Partition] targeting The One Ring. How many cards does Amiyah draw when the activated ability resolves?

Amiyah draws zero cards.

Then "draw a card for each burden counter on The One Ring" uses The One Ring's last known information from the battlefield (113.7a), which was zero burden counters. question: Nathaniel controls [Rest in Peace] and [Dauthi Voidwalker], and Armani casts [Read the Bones]. What happens to it?
answer:
Read the Bones resolves normally (Armani scries 2, draws two cards, loses 2 life), and then, instead of going to Armani's graveyard, Read the Bones is exiled. Armani — as the card's owner, since a spell on the stack heading to the graveyard has no controller once it finishes resolving — chooses which of the two replacement effects applies (616.1, 616.1f, 400.6).

Both Rest in Peace ("If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") and Dauthi Voidwalker ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it") are replacement effects trying to modify the same event — Read the Bones being put into Armani's graveyard (614.1). Neither is a self-replacement effect and neither changes control of a permanent entering the battlefield, so no effect is forced to be chosen first; the choice is free (614.15, 616.1a, 616.1b, 616.1e).

- If Armani picks Rest in Peace, Read the Bones is exiled with no counter, and the process repeats — but the graveyard event no longer happens, so Dauthi Voidwalker's effect does nothing (614.7, 616.1f).
- If Armani picks Dauthi Voidwalker, Read the Bones is exiled with a void counter on it, and Nathaniel can later tap and sacrifice Dauthi Voidwalker to cast Read the Bones without paying its mana cost that turn (subject to normal timing rules for sorceries).

So Armani will essentially always choose Rest in Peace, denying Nathaniel the void counter. Note Dauthi Voidwalker only applies because Armani is Nathaniel's opponent; Rest in Peace applies to everyone's cards.

Multiplayer note: this works the same at any number of players. If several players' cards were being put into graveyards simultaneously and multiple owners had to choose, those choices are made in APNAP order (101.4, 616.1).

question: Aspen control [Pulmonic Sliver]. They cast [Dihada's Ploy], discarding [Dregscape Sliver] on resolution. Can Aspen put Dregscape Sliver on top of their library?
answer:
No. Dregscape Sliver goes to Aspen's graveyard as normal.

Two reasons, both from Pulmonic Sliver's own text: (1) Pulmonic Sliver's static abilities affect Slivers on the battlefield, so a Sliver card sitting in Aspen's hand isn't granted the ability at all; and (2) even the wording of the granted ability, "If this permanent would be put into a graveyard, you may put it on top of its owner's library instead," only applies to a permanent. A card in hand is not a permanent — it's just a card — so discarding Dregscape Sliver from hand isn't a permanent being put into a graveyard and the replacement effect has nothing to replace. (Compare Pulmonic Sliver ruling #3, which frames the effect around Slivers that would die, i.e. be put into a graveyard from the battlefield.) Card text controls here, and it simply doesn't cover discards.

Assumed timing: Dihada's Ploy's own instruction "Draw two cards, then discard a card" happens during its resolution, and Aspen chooses Dregscape Sliver then. Note that no player receives priority in the middle of a spell's resolution, so Aspen can't take actions between the draws and the discard (117.1, 608.1, 608.2n); the discard just happens, and Dregscape Sliver lands in the graveyard.

Upside: that discarded Dregscape Sliver counts toward Dihada's Ploy's life gain (Dihada's Ploy ruling #0 — it counts the card discarded as part of its effect, plus any discarded earlier this turn, including a jump-start discard if Aspen cast it from the graveyard). And once Dregscape Sliver is in the graveyard it's not on the battlefield, so per Dregscape Sliver ruling #2 it isn't granting unearth to other Sliver cards from there — though its own printed unearth {2} still lets Aspen return Dregscape Sliver itself from the graveyard.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Arely controls a [Barony Vampire]. Nico controls a [Trained Jackal]. Arely casts [Prey Upon], targeting the Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal. In response, Nico casts [Hanabi Blast], targeting the Barony Vampire. What happens?
answer:
Hanabi Blast resolves first and kills Barony Vampire, and then Prey Upon does nothing at all.

Step by step:

1. Nico's Hanabi Blast was cast while Prey Upon was already on the stack, so it resolves first [117.7]. It deals 2 damage to Barony Vampire, a 3/2, which is lethal, so Barony Vampire dies and goes to Arely's graveyard.
2. As part of Hanabi Blast's own resolution, Hanabi Blast returns to its owner's hand and then its controller (Nico, assuming Nico owns it) discards a card at random. If Arely owned that Hanabi Blast, it would return to Arely's hand and Nico would still be the one discarding at random [Hanabi Blast ruling #0].
3. Prey Upon then tries to resolve. Barony Vampire is no longer on the battlefield, so it is an illegal target — a target that no longer exists or no longer meets the spell's specifications [Illegal Target] [608.2b]. Trained Jackal is still a legal target, but Prey Upon requires both.
4. Because one of Prey Upon's targets is illegal on resolution, no creature deals or is dealt damage [Prey Upon ruling #0]. Trained Jackal is untouched and survives. (Note that under 608.2b a spell only fails to resolve entirely if *all* its targets are illegal; here Trained Jackal is still legal, so Prey Upon does resolve but its fight instruction accomplishes nothing per its ruling.) Prey Upon is then put into Arely's graveyard as the final part of its resolution [608.2n].

Timing assumption: the question says Hanabi Blast was cast "in response," so it is above Prey Upon on the stack and resolves first. If instead Nico had somehow only cast Hanabi Blast after Prey Upon finished resolving, Prey Upon's fight would have happened first — Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal would deal 3 and 1 damage to each other, killing Trained Jackal, and Hanabi Blast's 2 damage would then finish off Barony Vampire.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Annabel controls [Altar of Dementia] and casts [Too Greedily, Too Deep] returning Nolan's [Sepulchral Primordial] to the battlefield. Can Annabel use Altar of Dementia to sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial and return it to the battlefield using its own triggered ability?
answer:
No. Sepulchral Primordial cannot bring itself back with its own enters-the-battlefield trigger.

Why: Too Greedily, Too Deep puts Sepulchral Primordial onto the battlefield under Annabel's control, and its triggered ability ("When this creature enters, for each opponent, you may put up to one target creature card from that player's graveyard onto the battlefield under your control") triggers. Targets for a triggered ability are chosen when the ability is put on the stack, which happens the next time a player would receive priority — and at that moment Sepulchral Primordial is on the battlefield, not in anyone's graveyard, so it is not a legal target [113.7a]. There is no window in which Annabel can activate Altar of Dementia ("Sacrifice a creature: Target player mills cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power") before the trigger's targets are locked in, because she only gets priority after the trigger is already on the stack with its targets chosen.

If Annabel instead sacrifices Sepulchral Primordial to Altar of Dementia after the trigger is on the stack (putting the card into Nolan's graveyard, since a card goes to its owner's graveyard), that does nothing to help: the trigger will resolve doing only what it can for the targets it already has, and it cannot pick up a card that wasn't targeted [603.6]. Zone-change triggers look for objects in the zone the object moved to, and a card that changes zones becomes a new object with no relation to its earlier existence [400.7], so nothing retroactively makes Sepulchral Primordial a target.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, "for each opponent" lets Annabel choose one target creature card in each opponent's graveyard, including Nolan's — but the same restriction applies, since Sepulchral Primordial isn't in a graveyard when targets are chosen. In a two-player game only Nolan's graveyard is eligible. In either case Annabel could sacrifice a different creature to Altar of Dementia and mill Nolan, but Sepulchral Primordial still can't reanimate itself.

question: Ari casts [Memories Returning]. Does Noor have a chance to exile it with [Dawnhand Dissident] before Ari can cast Memories Returning again for its flashback cost?
answer:
No — assuming Ari has the mana and casts it right away, Noor gets no window. Ari can cast Memories Returning from the graveyard for its Flashback {7}{U}{U} before Noor ever receives priority.

Why:

1. While Memories Returning is on the stack the first time, Dawnhand Dissident's "{T}, Blight 2: Exile target card from a graveyard" has no legal target for it — Memories Returning is a spell on the stack, not a card in a graveyard (a spell is a card on the stack, [112.1]). Noor can respond to the spell ([117.7]), but not exile it.
2. Memories Returning resolves and is put into Ari's graveyard. Ari, as the player whose turn it is, receives priority at that point before any opponent can act — Memories Returning ruling #2 states this directly: "If a card with flashback is put into your graveyard during your turn, you can cast it if it's legal to do so before any other player can take any actions." With priority ([117.1a]) and an empty stack in Ari's main phase (flashback still obeys sorcery timing, Memories Returning ruling #0), Ari legally casts it from the graveyard by paying {7}{U}{U} instead of {2}{U}{U} ([702.34a], Memories Returning ruling #4). Once it's cast, Ari keeps priority ([601.2i]).
3. Now Memories Returning is on the stack again and again untargetable by Dawnhand Dissident's exile ability. And it won't matter: a spell cast with flashback is exiled no matter how it leaves the stack (Memories Returning ruling #3).

When Noor DOES get a chance: if Ari can't or doesn't cast it immediately and passes priority, or if Ari's main phase has ended, or Ari casts something else first, then Noor may activate "{T}, Blight 2" while Memories Returning sits in Ari's graveyard and exile it, denying the flashback. Note Dawnhand Dissident's last ability (casting creature spells from exile during your turn) is irrelevant here — Memories Returning is a sorcery.

Timing assumption: I read the question as Ari intending to flash it back at the first opportunity in the same main phase. If instead Ari waits (e.g., taps out, or the turn moves on), Noor's window opens as described above.

Two players vs. more: the answer is the same at any table size. Ari, the active player, receives priority first after Memories Returning resolves, so no opponent — whether one or several — gets to act in between ([117.1a], Memories Returning ruling #2).

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
No — Coral Commando stops attacking. Gaining control of an attacking creature removes it from combat: a permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. So when Flash Conscription resolves and Arely takes control of Coral Commando, Coral Commando is no longer an attacking creature, deals no combat damage in the combat damage step, and any blocker assigned to it becomes blocking nothing.

This is true even though Aubrey and Arely are teammates in Two-Headed Giant. In shared team turns, the active team declares one combined attack and announces what each creature is attacking [805.10b], but control is still tracked per player, not per team, so a teammate taking control of Coral Commando is a controller change and triggers removal from combat [506.4a].

A few knock-on points:
- Coral Commando already "attacked" for purposes of any abilities that triggered on attackers being declared; those triggers happened at declaration and are unaffected [508.2a], [508.3c]. Removing it from combat later doesn't undo them.
- Spells or abilities that would have kept Coral Commando from attacking wouldn't remove it from combat, but a control change specifically does [506.4a].
- Timing assumption: I'm reading Flash Conscription as cast after attackers were declared (during the declare attackers step, once the active player had priority [508.2a]). If instead it were cast before attackers were declared, Arely would simply control Coral Commando, and since a creature can only attack if its controller is an attacking player, it would be Arely's creature to declare (in 2HG, part of the team's combined attack) rather than being removed from combat.
- Untapping and haste from Flash Conscription don't put Coral Commando back into combat; nothing here states it's attacking, which is what would be required to make it an attacking creature again [508.4].

question: Axel controls [Vastwood Gorger] and attacks Nico's [Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset]. Before damage is dealt, Nico activates [Barrin, Master Wizard], sacrificing Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset. Does Vastwood Gorger deal damage? If so, to what?
answer:
Vastwood Gorger deals no combat damage at all (assuming it is unblocked and stays on the battlefield).

When Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset is sacrificed as part of the cost of Barrin, Master Wizard's ability, it leaves the battlefield and is therefore removed from combat — a permanent removed from combat has no further involvement in that combat phase [506.4], [Remove from Combat]. Removing the attacked planeswalker does not remove Vastwood Gorger from combat: Vastwood Gorger continues to be an attacking creature, but it is attacking no player, planeswalker, or battle, it may still be blocked, and if it is unblocked it deals no combat damage [506.4c]. The combat damage rules confirm this: an unblocked creature assigns damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking, and if it isn't currently attacking anything — for example, because the planeswalker it was attacking left the battlefield — it assigns no combat damage [510.1b].

Vastwood Gorger has no trample, so none of its damage can be redirected to Nico; rule [702.19f] states that a creature without trample over planeswalkers that was attacking a planeswalker can assign no combat damage to the defending player even if that planeswalker has been removed from combat. (Only "trample over planeswalkers" would let the damage go to Nico, and even then it would not count as attacking Nico [702.19e].)

Timing note: I'm assuming Barrin, Master Wizard's ability resolves before the combat damage step. If instead combat damage had already been dealt to Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset, that damage would have counted and the sacrifice afterward would change nothing about the damage already dealt. Also note Barrin, Master Wizard's ability returns a target *creature* to its owner's hand; if Nico targeted Vastwood Gorger itself, Vastwood Gorger would leave the battlefield and likewise be removed from combat and deal no damage [506.4].

This works the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game; the relevant "defending player" is determined per attacking creature as the controller of the planeswalker it was attacking [508.5].
